content.title: Military draft 2026? Are high school and college students eligible?
content.text: April 9, 2026, 4:08 p.m. ETAs concerns about a US military draft spread online and across campuses amid President Donald Trump's war in Iran, students and parents are asking the same questions: could high school seniors or college students be drafted if the military draft returns? With new attention on automatic Selective Service rules and new draft age limits, confusion and anxiety is rising fast.Here's what to know about draft and enlistment ages, how Selective Service registration impacts 18-year-old high school and college students, enrollment requirements, who can defer and who would be exempt.The Army announced last month it would raise the maximum age for eligible recruits to 42, while removing obstacles for recruits who had single marijuana or drug paraphernalia convictions. The change takes effect April 20, 2026, the Army memo states. The upper limit of the Army's previous allowable enlistment age was 35.While no draft has been called, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt has said the president was not ruling out a military draft as the US-Iran ceasefire hits tenuous ground, with Trump threatening "shooting stars" if Iran backs out of a deal.The last time a draft was called in the US was in 1972 during the Vietnam War. At this time, neither Congress nor Trump has reinstated the war, which requires legislation.Is there an automatic military draft?No, there is not an automatic military draft in 2026. Automatic Selective Service registration is beginning on Dec. 18, 2026, which will automate registration of eligible men should a draft be called. It does not activate a draft.Currently, registration for Selective Service in the US is required for all men within 30 days of turning 18, or for those entering the US between ages 18-25. Registration does not mean you are being drafted, but it places you in a contingency database, according to the Selective Service System.What age are you eligible for the draft? US military draft age rangeUS men are eligible for the draft when they turn 18, regardless of whether they are in college or high school. The age you are no longer eligible? Once you turn 26, you are no longer required to register for Selective Service, meaning you will not be drafted, barring any changes that Congress can make when drafting legislation.Are college students exempt from the draft?College students are not exempt from a military draft in the US, though they can get temporary postponement to finish a college semester. All men are required to register within 30 days of their 18th birthday for Selective Service, though come Dec. 18, 2026, the process will switch to automatic SS registration.According to the Selective Service System, a temporary deferment would only last while the student remains enrolled. Congress, however, could change those rules should the need for military power rise.Student deferments were eliminated in the early 1970s. During the Vietnam-era, many college students received deferments, which was heavily criticized and eventually ended in 1971 by President Nixon, according to the Harvard Crimson.Can high school students be drafted?Yes, high school students can be drafted once they turn 18, meaning you can be a high school senior (or even junior), register for Selective Service and be called upon to go through the draft selection process. This includes students in public or private high schools, or vocational or trade schools in any state.What makes you exempt from the draft?Women or people born female, those 26 years old or older, and those in prison or jail, hospitalized or institutionalized are exempt from the draft, according to the Selective Service eligibility chart. Further, certain medical or mental conditions may disqualify a person during the intake process (MEPS exam), and full-time clergy members and ministers are disqualified.What happens if you don't register for the draft?Registering with the Selective Service is required regardless of college enrollment, and failing to register is actually a federal felony, punishable by up to 5 years in prison and/or $250,000 in fines. It can affect federal student financial aid, federal employment eligibility and some state benefits. It would also block or delay the naturalization process.How to register for selective serviceHead to the Selective Service website and go through the Register Now process. Not sure if you are registered for Selective Service? Head to sss.gov/verify, input your last name, Social Security number and date of birth.Lori Comstock is a New Jersey-based news reporter covering trending news with USA TODAY Network's Mid-Atlantic Connect Team. She covers news in the Northeast, including New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Washington DC, Maryland, and Virginia. Reach her at LComstock@usatodayco.com.
